claims.text: The material family of interest is multiphase refractory high-entropy alloys.
The primary mechanical property of interest is room-temperature tensile ductility.
The initial alloy has a disordered BCC or BCC+Laves multiphase microstructure.
The proposed intervention is isothermal aging at 500–800 °C for approximately 100–1000 hours.
Intermediate-temperature aging produces a ductile-to-brittle-to-ductile transition rather than a monotonic change in tensile ductility.
Initial aging forms brittle ordered intermetallic phases such as B2 or L12.
The initially formed ordered phases impede dislocation motion and promote crack initiation, thereby reducing ductility.
Continued aging causes coherent, nanoscale ordered precipitates to nucleate and grow.
Coherent SCCP interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission.
Coherent SCCP interfaces relieve stress concentrations associated with premature crack initiation.
Dislocations cut through or bypass the precipitates by shearing or Orowan looping.
Formation of coherent nanoscale precipitates during continued aging restores tensile ductility.
At 200–400 hours of aging, tensile ductility decreases by more than 50% relative to the as-processed state.
After more than 600 hours of aging, tensile elongation recovers to at least 10% and becomes comparable to or greater than its initial value.
The late-aging ductility recovery is accompanied by a peak in yield strength.
The as-processed baseline alloy has approximately 10–15% tensile elongation and high strength.
The non-monotonic transition is confined to a 500–800 °C aging window in which ordering is kinetically active but coarsening has not dominated.
Below the proposed aging-temperature window, chemical ordering is too slow to produce the transition.
Above the proposed aging-temperature window, precipitates coarsen or dissolve and the coherent strengthening mechanism is eliminated.
Supporting the hypothesis requires identifying the ordered phases, correlating their appearance with the ductility minimum, and demonstrating coherent interfaces in the recovered state.
